title: Buyers for the first time behind more than half of all sales of mortgaged housing last year to reach a new record
text:
Buyers for the first time were behind more than half of all mortgaged housing sales last year, according to Halifax
The buyers market for the first time was recovered last year, according to the mortgage lender, with 19 percent more people on the ladder than in 2023.
In total, the number of people who bought a property for the first time increased to 341,068 last year, compared to 287,060 in 2023.
Halifax said first -time buyers represented 54 percent of all mortgaged housing purchases last year, the largest registered majority.
Much of this was probably due to a more stable mortgage market, and rates are widely maintained between 4 and 5 percent for most of 2024.
Despite the challenges to save for a deposit and the increase in housing prices, first -time buyers still represent more than half of all new mortgages, the greatest majority registered
Between the beginning of July and October last year, the lower five -year fixed rate mortgage fell from 4.28 percent to a minimum of 3.68 percent.
Meanwhile, the lowest two -year solution fell from 4.68 percent to a minimum of 3.84 percent, although rates have increased since then.
This represented an improvement of the chaos of 2023, where a combination of base rates and concerns on inflation saw that the average fixed rates of two years reached a maximum of 6.86 percent in the summer, according to Moneyfacts, while the rates of Five years reached 6.35 for each penny.
Amanda Bryden, director of mortgages in Halifax, said: ‘Last year he saw a great increase in the number of first -time buyers, almost a fifth since 2023.
“This probably reflects an improvement in the affordability of the mortgage, since interest rates decreased and stabilized, providing more certainty for those who step on the stairs.”
The increase in buyer activity for the first time has probably also driven by the fact that many are aware that bell tax costs will increase from April 1.
As of April 1, the timbre fees rate threshold for buyers for the first time will fall from £ 425,000 to £ 300,000.
As a result, a buyer for the first time buys a house with a price of between £ 300,000 and £ 500,000 will face a 5 percent timbre tax charge in an additional loan of £ 125,000, adding thousands of pounds to the general cost.
This means that instead of not paying any bell tax in a purchase worth £ 425,000, since April they will soon pay £ 6,205.
Santander reported that he saw a 130 percent increase in mortgage requests in the last three months of 2024 compared to the same period in 2023.
The mortgage lender reduces this increase to a large extent to buyers who rush to ensure a purchase of property before the changes of bell tax.
Graham Selar, head of the intermediary channel for mortgages in Santander said: “We all know that buying a house, whether our first or our house forever, comes with significant costs.”
‘Each penny counts when considering things like the legal and costs of moving, so it is great to see so many people take full advantage of holidays and ensure their new home before April 1;
How do buyers work for the first time? Even with the mortgage rates that are around 4 and 5 percent for most buyers, this represents a much more challenging situation than in years before 2022 when rates were between 1 and 2 percent for the most part.
With the average values ​​of the properties for buyers for the first time now around 6.6 times the average salary is a difficult task that a house is alone.
The new buyers are depositing £ 61,090 on average with the typical typical starting house that costs £ 311,034 last year.
Therefore, many are associated with another person. Almost two thirds Of the end of the mortgage last year they were in two or more names, according to Halifax.
There is also the fact that buyers for the first time are saving for a longer time. The average buyer for the first time in 2024 was 33 years old, which is two years older than a decade ago.
Buyer for the first time Jemma with her husband Tom and her children Leo and Lucas
Jemma Sparrow, 40, from Chipping Sodbury in South Gloudeshire arrived at the property staircase for the first time last year.
“After renting for years, it was always our dream to have a house to call ours,” Jemma said.
‘However, it has been a challenge, especially with my husband worked on his own. Balancing the rent, raising our children and being able to leave enough money for a deposit was difficult.
‘We were always looking for ways to save extra money. Finally, last November, just before turning 40, we were able to buy our house forever.
‘I still can’t believe that it is really ours and much larger than the previous houses we rent. My favorite part is being able to decorate it and change things exactly how we want. ‘
